newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia warns Taleban to respect Afghan frontier.
newsitem.headline: Russia warns Taleban to respect Afghan frontier.

text.p: Russia warned the Taleban militia on Tuesday it would respond to any breach of the old Soviet-Afghan frontier, after the militantly Islamic group seized control of much of the north of Afghanistan.
Russian officials also met diplomats from Central Asia and other former Soviet member states of a regional defence pact to assess the threat to their security along the Afghan border.

"Russia and its Central Asian partners are seriously worried by the potential threat to the southern borders of the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States)," Russian foreign ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov told a regular news briefing.

"I want to reiterate earlier statements that if the borders are violated then measures under the Collective Security Treaty will be undertaken," he said, adding that, for now, Moscow saw the Taleban advance as an internal Afghan matter.

Diplomats from nine of the 12 ex-Soviet member states of the CIS attended a meeting in Moscow of signatories of the 1992 Collective Security Treaty, which provides for mutual military assistance in the event of external aggression.

A statement by the body's executive said the diplomats discussed convening a meeting of deputy ministers on the Afghan situation and also whether to summon the Collective Security Council, the group's top-level political organ.
It did not say if any decision was made. Interfax news agency quoted unnamed sources as saying Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev had proposed a summit of the pact's members in his capital Almaty.

The sudden collapse of opposition to the Taleban militia in northern Afghanistan, allowing it to sweep close to the old Soviet frontier, has sparked alarm in Moscow and across the region at the spread of fundamentalist Islam.
Russia and its neighbours also fear a wave of refugees and defeated anti-Taleban fighters could destabilise countries like Tajikistan in formerly Soviet Central Asia.

Four of the five former Soviet states in Central Asia -- Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan -- are signatories with Russia of the Collective Security Treaty, which came into force in 1994. Turkmenistan, which with Tajikistan and Uzbekistan actually borders Afghanistan, is not a member.
Belarus and the Caucasus states of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia are signatories.
Russia has some 20,000 troops and frontier guards in Tajikistan, where they guard the Afghan border and police a fragile peace that is holding after four years of civil war.
Those forces and the troops of some Central Asian states near the mountainous Afghan frontier have been placed on alert following the rapid Taleban advance at the weekend.

Along the Amu Darya, or Oxus, river dividing Uzbekistan from Afghanistan, Uzbekistan's troops dug trenches on Tuesday and a lone tank stood guard on Friendship Bridge, which the Soviet army crossed to invade Afghanistan in 1979 and to retreat, defeated, in 1989.
The Soviet Union, by official accounts, lost 13,000 troops in Afghanistan.
